scenes.tts: Two kinds of paramecium can each grow alone. What changes when they draw from one food supply? These tiny one-celled living things swim through two clear tubes. Gold food dots drift through both tubes. Teal swimmers fill one tube, while coral swimmers fill the other.
scenes.visual: Hook picture, no title yet. COLOR MAP for this film: limited resource GOLD, aurelia TEAL, caudatum CORAL, cooperation GREEN, abiotic factor BLUE. Film 2 keeps GOLD, GREEN and BLUE, uses TEAL for the population it follows, and uses CORAL for living threats. Two large clear tubes fill most of the frame. Gold food dots drift downward continuously. Teal and coral paramecium cartoons swim with beating edge marks; each population slowly multiplies. Put the question above the tubes in large white text.
scenes.narration: Two kinds of paramecium can each grow alone. What changes when they draw from one food supply? These tiny one-celled living things swim through two clear tubes. Gold food dots drift through both tubes. Teal swimmers fill one tube, while coral swimmers fill the other.

scenes.visual: The two tubes slide together behind a brief title: One Tube, One Shared Supply. Food dots keep drifting; swimmers keep moving.

scenes.tts: A population is every member of one species in one place at one time. Each tube begins with one population and fresh food. As food arrives, each population grows. Soon the bars stop rising, because a steady supply cannot support endless growth.
scenes.visual: Keep the same tubes. Transform some swimmers into matching bars beside each tube, then continue adding swimmers and raising both bars. A small gold food gauge refills steadily. Both bars bend toward plateaus; label the animated lines schematic.
scenes.narration: A population is every member of one species in one place at one time. Each tube begins with one population and fresh food. As food arrives, each population grows. Soon the bars stop rising, because a steady supply cannot support endless growth.

scenes.tts: Competition happens when living things need the same resource and there is not enough for all. It does not require a fight. A food dot eaten by one swimmer simply disappears. That food is no longer available to another swimmer.
scenes.visual: Bring the tubes side by side until their walls touch. One gold food dot enters between a teal and coral swimmer. Teal reaches it first; the dot vanishes and coral turns away. Repeat slowly at different positions while both populations remain in motion.
scenes.narration: Competition happens when living things need the same resource and there is not enough for all. It does not require a fight. A food dot eaten by one swimmer simply disappears. That food is no longer available to another swimmer.

scenes.tts: Now slide both populations into one tube without adding more food. Which population will stay common? Which will fall? Make a prediction from the picture, then watch the real counts build.
scenes.visual: Merge the tubes into one wide tube. Keep the gold food gauge at the former single-tube level. Place two empty axes beside it, teal above coral. Show the question in large text while swimmers circle the shared food.
scenes.narration: Now slide both populations into one tube without adding more food. Which population will stay common? Which will fall? Make a prediction from the picture, then watch the real counts build.

scenes.visual: Deliberate thinking pause. Hold the question and empty axes. Gold food continues drifting and both swimmer colors circle slowly. Do not reveal any data.

scenes.tts: Gowse tested that comparison with bacteria as food. He grew each kind alone, then grew them together under the same conditions. Teal aurelia stayed common in the shared tube. Coral caudatum rose at first, then fell to a small population.
scenes.caption: Gause tested that comparison with bacteria as food. He grew each kind alone, then grew them together under the same conditions. Teal aurelia stayed common in the shared tube. Coral caudatum rose at first, then fell to a small population.
scenes.visual: Replace the empty axes with points from the lesson's Gause table, connected only to guide the eye. Numbers and day labels appear on screen but are not spoken. Label the plot Gause data, selected days. Teal sharing points rise and remain high. Coral sharing points rise, peak, then fall. A moving time cursor sweeps across both plots.
scenes.narration: Gause tested that comparison with bacteria as food. He grew each kind alone, then grew them together under the same conditions. Teal aurelia stayed common in the shared tube. Coral caudatum rose at first, then fell to a small population.

scenes.tts: The fair comparison is each population against itself. On the last day shown, sharing had held both kinds back, but caudatum much more. Caudatum lost a much larger share of its alone count. The data do not show either kind vanishing by the last day shown. Coral swimmers are still in the tube, but their count is still falling.
scenes.visual: At the last plotted day, draw a teal bracket between aurelia alone and sharing. Draw a coral bracket between caudatum alone and sharing. Show the lesson's four counts on screen. Then change each pair into a simple fraction bar; coral's remaining fraction is visibly much smaller. Keep swimmers moving faintly behind the plot.
scenes.narration: The fair comparison is each population against itself. On the last day shown, sharing had held both kinds back, but caudatum much more. Caudatum lost a much larger share of its alone count. The data do not show either kind vanishing by the last day shown. Coral swimmers are still in the tube, but their count is still falling.

scenes.tts: This is quiet competition. The paramecia do not chase or attack one another. They use the same limited food. Members of one species can compete too, because they often need the same resources in the same place.
scenes.visual: Return the data points into colored swimmers inside the shared tube. Remove any collision or attack marks. Gold dots disappear only when eaten. Duplicate the teal population alone in a second outline to show members of one species reaching the same food.
scenes.narration: This is quiet competition. The paramecia do not chase or attack one another. They use the same limited food. Members of one species can compete too, because they often need the same resources in the same place.

scenes.tts: The lesson's simulation is simpler than a real tube. Its food is steady, it has no predators, and one kind is set to use food faster. Gause also warned that other conditions in the liquid mattered. The counts support competition, but they cannot prove food was the only cause.
scenes.visual: Build three large schematic controls around the same tube: steady food gauge locked, predator icon crossed out, speed dial labelled model setting, turned toward one unlabelled swimmer shape. Do not tie the dial to teal or coral. Then place a question-mark badge labelled other liquid conditions beside the tube. Keep all swimmers and food drifting.
scenes.narration: The lesson's simulation is simpler than a real tube. Its food is steady, it has no predators, and one kind is set to use food faster. Gause also warned that other conditions in the liquid mattered. The counts support competition, but they cannot prove food was the only cause.

scenes.tts: Here is the lesson's rule. Limited resources can restrict populations; cooperation can help members meet their needs. This film built the first half. Limited resources can restrict populations, even without a fight. The second film asks what working together can change.
scenes.visual: Transform the shared tube into two balanced halves of one rule card. On the left, gold food divides between teal and coral swimmers. On the right, a green path begins connecting three neutral worker shapes without revealing their jobs. End with the left picture complete and the right picture waiting.
